pos: adj. & n. (foremost in order, rank, or time; rendering Hebrew ri'shon, Greek prōtos)
etymology: Saxon fyrst, superlative of fore. Scripture uses it three ways at once — first in sequence, first in rank, and First as a name of God.
biblical_def: First in Scripture is never merely the head of a list. It is an ordering God imposes and a title God claims. Christ says of Himself, “I am the first and the last” (Rev 1:17), and again, “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last” (Rev 22:13) — language the LORD had already used of Himself in Isaiah, so that the risen Christ is naming His own deity. Under that title everything else is sequenced. There is a first commandment, and our Lord identifies it: love to God with the whole heart is “the first and great commandment” (Mat 22:38), which means the whole moral law hangs on an order, not merely a list. There is a first man: “The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit” (1Co 15:45) — two federal heads, and every soul that has ever lived stands under one or the other. To be first in Scripture is therefore to be representative, to be determinative, to carry the rest along. This is why the firstborn is consecrated, why the firstfruits are brought before the harvest is touched, and why the kingdom must be sought first (Mat 6:33). The order is not arbitrary. God has arranged reality with a first, and to invert it is idolatry.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines first as advanced before or further than any other in progression, place, rank, dignity, or time — the ordinal of one.
webster_full: FIRST, a. Advanced before or further than any other in progression; foremost in place; as the first man in a marching column.
2. Preceding all others in the order of time.
3. Preceding all others in numbers or a progressive series; the ordinal of one.
4. Preceding others in rank, dignity or excellence; chief; principal.
scriptures: Rev 1:17
And when I saw him, I fell at his feet as dead. And he laid his right hand upon me, saying unto me, Fear not; I am the first and the last:
I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last.
This is the first and great commandment.
And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit.
corruption_summary: An age that has abolished rank has abolished first as a category — keeping the word for what happens earliest while denying that anything is owed the place of chief.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern usage keeps first as a stopwatch word and empties it of authority: first is whoever got there soonest, not what holds the place of chief by right. Scripture uses it the other way around. The first commandment is not first because Moses wrote it at the top of the tablet; it is first because God is God. Where the ordinal is flattened into mere sequence, the first commandment becomes one value among several to be balanced, and the balancing is done by the man doing the weighing — which is precisely the second commandment's definition of an idol.

The other loss is federal. “The first man Adam” is not an interesting datum about early history; he is the head under whom the race fell, and unless he is the real first man there is no coherent account of why we die or of how one Man's obedience could answer for many. Recover the ordinal and the gospel's logic returns: a first Adam who lost us, a last Adam who is a quickening spirit, and a first-and-last Christ who was dead and is alive for evermore.
roots_summary: Hebrew ri'shon (H7223), first, chief, former; Greek prōtos (G4413), first in time, place, order, or importance — and the divine title in Revelation.
roots_lines: Hebrew ri'shon (H7223) — first, foremost, former; used of the first month (Exo 12:2), the first day, and the LORD as first (Isa 44:6).
Greek prōtos (G4413) — first in order or in rank; the first commandment (Mar 12:30), the first resurrection (Rev 20:5), and “I am the first and the last” (Rev 1:17).
Greek archē (G746) — beginning, origin, first place; paired with telos (end) in the title of Rev 22:13.
usage: “I am the first and the last” — the ordinal used as a divine name.
“This is the first and great commandment” — the moral law has an order, and love to God heads it.
“The first man Adam” — federal headship stated as a sequence.

pos: adj. & n. (next after the first in order or rank; rendering Hebrew sheni, Greek deuteros)
etymology: From Latin secundus, following, from sequi, to follow. In Scripture the second is rarely a mere repetition; it is the answer to the first, and often its undoing or its fulfilment.
biblical_def: Scripture's seconds are decisive. There is a second death: “And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death” (Rev 20:14), and John names its inhabitants — the fearful, the unbelieving, the abominable, and all liars (Rev 21:8). The first death separates soul from body; the second separates soul and body from God for ever, and it is this, not the grave, that the gospel saves from. There is a second man: “The first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven” (1Co 15:47) — and there will be no third, because the second is the last Adam and needs no successor. And there is a second appearing: “unto them that look for him shall he appear the second time without sin unto salvation” (Heb 9:28). The first coming dealt with sin by the sacrifice of Himself; the second has no sin-bearing left to do and is therefore pure salvation to those who look for Him. So the pattern holds: the second death answers the first sin, the second Man answers the first Adam, and the second advent answers the first. Which second a soul meets is settled by whether it belongs to the second Man.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines second as immediately following the first in order of place or time, next in value, power, excellence, or rank — and as the act of supporting another.
webster_full: SECOND, a. Immediately following the first; next to the first in order of place or time.
2. Next in value, power, excellence, dignity or rank; inferior.
3. Being of the same kind as another that has preceded; another, as a second Cato.
scriptures: And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death.
Rev 21:8

But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death.
The first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven.
Heb 9:28
So Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many; and unto them that look for him shall he appear the second time without sin unto salvation.
corruption_summary: Second chance has been made a doctrine the Bible never teaches — a second offer beyond death — while the second death Scripture does teach is quietly dropped from the preaching.
corruption_paragraphs: The confusion is exact and it inverts the text. Scripture speaks of a second death; the modern religious imagination speaks of a second chance, and locates it after dying. There is no such promise. “It is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27) stands in the very context of Christ's second appearing, and the lake of fire in Revelation 20 is described as final, not probationary. Universalism and post-mortem-opportunity teaching both trade on the word second and both empty the second death of its finality; the 1689 Confession, following the whole Reformed line, holds eternal conscious punishment because the text does.

The second loss is in preaching. Where the second death is not named, the first death becomes the worst thing that can happen to a man, and the gospel shrinks into consolation for the bereaved. Recover Revelation's ordinal and the proportions return: the grave is the lesser enemy, already conquered; the lake of fire is the greater; and Hebrews' second appearing is the believer's hope precisely because the second death has no power over those who are in the second Man.
roots_summary: Hebrew sheni (H8145), second, again; Greek deuteros (G1208), second in order — the second death, the second man, and the second time He shall appear.
roots_lines: Hebrew sheni (H8145) — second, other, again; the second day of creation (Gen 1:8) and the second year of a reign.
Greek deuteros (G1208) — second; second death (Rev 20:14), second man (1Co 15:47), second time (Heb 9:28).
The pattern is federal, not merely numerical: what the first head lost, the second Head recovers (Rom 5:19).
usage: “This is the second death” — the final, conscious, irrevocable separation from God.
“The second man is the Lord from heaven” — and there is no third head of the race.
“He shall appear the second time without sin unto salvation” — the sin-bearing is finished.

pos: adj. & n. (next after the second; rendering Hebrew shelishi, Greek tritos)
etymology: Saxon thridda, from three. Scripture's third is the day of deliverance — the point at which the LORD turns death into life.
biblical_def: The third day is the Bible's appointed hour of resurrection, and the apostles preach it as prophecy fulfilled, not coincidence: “And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures” (1Co 15:4). Our Lord Himself grounds it in the Old Testament: “thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day” (Luk 24:46). Hosea had said it plainly of the LORD's dealings with His people — “After two days will he revive us: in the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight” (Hos 6:2) — and the pattern runs back further still, to the third day on which Abraham lifted his eyes and saw the mount where the son would be given and received back as from the dead. Paul also names a third heaven (2Co 12:2), the immediate presence of God above the visible sky and the starry expanse, into which he was caught up. So the ordinal carries two freights: the third day, when God raises; and the third heaven, where God dwells. Both say the same thing about Him. He does not leave His own in the grave, and He is not contained by what we can see.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines third as the ordinal of three — the first after the second, and the third part of anything divided into three.
webster_full: THIRD, a. The ordinal of three; the first after the second.
2. Containing or being one part of three into which any thing is divided.
THIRD, n. The third part of any thing.
scriptures: And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures:
And said unto them, Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day:
Hos 6:2
After two days will he revive us: in the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight.
I knew a man in Christ above fourteen years ago, (whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;) such an one caught up to the third heaven.
corruption_summary: Treated as a stray detail of the creed, the third day is in fact one of the load-bearing claims of the gospel — a dated, public, falsifiable event, not a symbol of renewal.
corruption_paragraphs: The chief corruption is to spiritualise the ordinal: the third day becomes an emblem of hope, of new beginnings, of the resilience of life, and the tomb becomes optional. Paul allows no such reading. He stakes the entire faith on the datable event — buried, and raised the third day, and seen — and says that if it did not happen we are of all men most miserable. A resurrection that means renewal-in-general is not the apostolic message; it is the message emptied and then praised for being inspiring.

The second error runs the other way, into curiosity: hunting the number three through Scripture for hidden codes. The text's own use is soberer and better. Hosea gives the shape of God's dealings — He wounds and He binds up, He kills and He makes alive, and the third day is when He raises. That is a pastoral doctrine for the afflicted saint, not a cipher. Recover it as history first, and it will preach as comfort second.
roots_summary: Hebrew shelishi (H7992), third; Greek tritos (G5154), third — the third day of the resurrection and the third heaven of God's immediate presence.
roots_lines: Hebrew shelishi (H7992) — third; the third day of Abraham's journey to Moriah (Gen 22:4) and Hosea's third day of raising (Hos 6:2).
Greek tritos (G5154) — third; “the third day he shall rise again” (Mat 20:19), and the third heaven of 2Co 12:2.
The apostolic formula “according to the scriptures” ties the ordinal to prophecy, not to accident.
usage: “He rose again the third day according to the scriptures” — the creed's date, and the gospel's hinge.
“In the third day he will raise us up” — the LORD's settled pattern with His people.
“Caught up to the third heaven” — the presence of God above every visible height.

pos: adj. & n. (next after the third; rendering Hebrew revi'i, Greek tetartos)
etymology: Saxon feortha, from four. In Scripture the fourth marks the darkest watch, the fourth figure in the fire, and the outer limit of visited iniquity.
biblical_def: The fourth in Scripture repeatedly names the point of extremity, and then the mercy that meets it there. The night was divided into four watches, and it was “in the fourth watch of the night” — the last and coldest, between three and dawn — that “Jesus went unto them, walking on the sea” (Mat 14:25); He came not at the first sign of labour but at the end of it. In Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar looks into the furnace and counts one too many: “the form of the fourth is like the Son of God” (Dan 3:25) — the fourth is the One who goes into the fire with His own. The second commandment sets a fourth as the boundary of visited iniquity, the LORD “visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me” (Exo 20:5) — a real covenantal reach through a family line, and yet bounded, while mercy runs to thousands. And in the Revelation the fourth seal releases the pale horse, the last and worst of the riders (Rev 6:7). Extremity, presence, boundary: the fourth teaches that the Lord is not absent at the end of the night, nor outside the fire, nor careless of generations.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fourth as the ordinal of four — the next after the third — and as one part of a thing divided into four.
webster_full: FOURTH, a. The ordinal of four; the next after the third.
2. Being one part of four into which any thing is divided.
FOURTH, n. A quarter; one of four equal parts.
scriptures: And in the fourth watch of the night Jesus went unto them, walking on the sea.
Dan 3:25
He answered and said, Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God.
Exo 20:5

Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;
Rev 6:7
And when he had opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth beast say, Come and see.
corruption_summary: Generational language has been captured by therapeutic and political theories of inherited guilt; Scripture's fourth generation is covenantal, bounded, and answered by a mercy that runs to thousands. <!-- voice-lock-ok: therapy: names the therapeutic frame in order to reject it -->
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 20 is now read through two foreign grids. One treats the fourth generation as a psychological inheritance — patterns passed down as damage rather than as sin — so that the descendant is a patient rather than a covenant-breaker who must repent. The other treats it as collective racial guilt, an inherited debt owed by a bloodline. Neither is the text. The LORD names the visited generations as “them that hate me”: the visitation follows the continued hatred, not the bloodline as such, and Ezekiel 18 states flatly that the son who turns shall not die for the father's iniquity. <!-- voice-lock-ok: therapy: rebuttal context -->

What the passage does teach is sobering and is usually the part omitted: sin genuinely runs in households, and a man's idolatry lays a weight on children he will never meet. The remedy Scripture gives is not a theory of inheritance but a covenant — the same verse-pair promises mercy unto thousands of them that love Him and keep His commandments. Four generations of judgment against a thousand of mercy is not a balance; it is a landslide, and it is the reason a converted father is the best thing that can happen to a family line.
roots_summary: Hebrew revi'i (H7243), fourth; Greek tetartos (G5067), fourth — the fourth watch, the fourth in the furnace, the fourth generation, the fourth seal.
roots_lines: Hebrew revi'i (H7243) — fourth; the fourth day of creation (Gen 1:19) and the fourth generation of Exo 20:5.
Greek tetartos (G5067) — fourth; the fourth watch (Mat 14:25) and the fourth seal (Rev 6:7).
The Roman night was reckoned in four watches, so the fourth is the hour before dawn — the point of greatest exhaustion.
usage: “In the fourth watch of the night Jesus went unto them” — He comes at the end of the rowing, not the beginning.
“The form of the fourth is like the Son of God” — the furnace is not a place He declines to enter.
“Unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me” — bounded judgment against mercy unto thousands.

pos: adj. & n. (next after the fourth; rendering Hebrew chamishi, Greek pemptos)
etymology: Saxon fifta, from five. The fifth part is Scripture's standard surcharge in restitution — the extra fifth that makes repentance cost something.
biblical_def: The fifth appears in Scripture chiefly as a measure of restitution and of patience. Under the law, a man who trespassed in a holy thing “shall add the fifth part thereto, and give it unto the priest” (Lev 5:16): the wrong is repaid, and a fifth is added on top, so that repentance is never merely the return of what was stolen but costs the sinner more than the sin gained him. Zacchaeus understood this instinct when he offered fourfold. The fifth also measures the LORD's patience with a planted land: the fruit of a new tree is uncircumcised three years, holy in the fourth, “and in the fifth year shall ye eat of the fruit thereof” (Lev 19:25) — God teaches a farmer to wait four years before he eats. In the Revelation the fifth seal uncovers the altar: “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9), the martyrs crying How long. And in the wall of the city the fifth foundation is sardonyx (Rev 21:20), the ordinals of the jewels showing that even the New Jerusalem is built in an order God counted out.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fifth as the ordinal of five, and as one part of a thing divided into five equal parts — the biblical surcharge in restitution.
webster_full: FIFTH, a. The ordinal of five; the next to the fourth.
2. Elliptically, a fifth part.
FIFTH, n. In music, an interval consisting of three tones and a semitone.
scriptures: Lev 5:16

And he shall make amends for the harm that he hath done in the holy thing, and shall add the fifth part thereto, and give it unto the priest: and the priest shall make an atonement for him with the ram of the trespass offering, and it shall be forgiven him.
And in the fifth year shall ye eat of the fruit thereof, that it may yield unto you the increase thereof: I am the LORD your God.
Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
The fifth, sardonyx; the sixth, sardius; the seventh, chrysolite; the eighth, beryl; the ninth, a topaz; the tenth, a chrysoprasus; the eleventh, a jacinth; the twelfth, an amethyst.
corruption_summary: Restitution has fallen almost entirely out of modern repentance, which asks for an apology where the law required the principal returned and a fifth added.
corruption_paragraphs: The added fifth is the part the modern conscience skips. Repentance is now widely understood as sorrow expressed and, at most, an apology accepted; the law of Leviticus assumed that a genuine turning would show up in the offender's purse. Restore the thing, add a fifth, bring the ram — sorrow, restitution, and sacrifice together. Where restitution is dropped, apology becomes cheap and the offended party is left carrying the loss while being asked to call the matter closed.

Nor is the fifth a rival to grace. The trespass offering stands in the same verse: the priest makes an atonement for him, and it shall be forgiven him. Blood forgives; the fifth part repairs. The gospel does not abolish the second by supplying the first — Zacchaeus met Christ and immediately began calculating repayment, and our Lord called that day salvation come to his house. A church that recovers the fifth will find its repentances harder and its reconciliations far more durable.
roots_summary: Hebrew chamishi (H2549), fifth, with chamishith, a fifth part; Greek pemptos (G3991), fifth — restitution, patience, and the martyrs' seal.
roots_lines: Hebrew chamishi (H2549) — fifth; the fifth year of Lev 19:25 and the fifth month of the temple's burning.
Hebrew chamishith — a fifth part; the surcharge added in restitution (Lev 5:16; Lev 6:5; Num 5:7).
Greek pemptos (G3991) — fifth; the fifth seal (Rev 6:9) and the fifth foundation stone (Rev 21:20).
usage: “Shall add the fifth part thereto” — repentance that costs more than the sin gained.
“In the fifth year shall ye eat of the fruit thereof” — God teaches His people to wait.
“When he had opened the fifth seal” — the altar, and the martyrs crying How long.

pos: adj. & n. (next after the fifth; rendering Hebrew shishshi, Greek hektos)
etymology: Saxon sixta, from six. The sixth is the day man was made and the hour the sun failed — the ordinal of humanity and of humanity's judgment fallen on Another.
biblical_def: The sixth day is the day of man. God made the beasts and then the man and the woman in His own image, “and God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day” (Gen 1:31) — the only day pronounced very good, and the day creation received its head and its steward. The sixth hour carries the counterpart. It was “about the sixth hour” that a wearied Christ sat on Jacob's well and asked a Samaritan woman for a drink (Joh 4:6), the Maker of the sixth day thirsty in the flesh He had made. And it was “from the sixth hour” that “there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour” (Mat 27:45) — at high noon, when the sun should have stood at full strength, God darkened it over the head of the race hanging on a tree. The sixth seal follows the same logic on a cosmic scale: earthquake, sun black as sackcloth, moon as blood (Rev 6:12). Man was made on the sixth; man's judgment fell at the sixth; and the whole created order will shake at the sixth.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sixth as the ordinal of six, the first after the fifth, and as one part of a thing divided into six equal parts.
webster_full: SIXTH, a. The ordinal of six; the first after the fifth.
2. Constituting or being one part of six into which a thing is divided.
SIXTH, n. A sixth part.
scriptures: Gen 1:31
And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.
Joh 4:6
Now Jacob's well was there. Jesus therefore, being wearied with his journey, sat thus on the well: and it was about the sixth hour.
Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour.
Rev 6:12
And I beheld when he had opened the sixth seal, and, lo, there was a great earthquake; and the sun became black as sackcloth of hair, and the moon became as blood;
corruption_summary: The sixth day is now read as a poetic gesture rather than a day, which costs the doctrine of man its foundation — if there was no sixth day there was no first Adam, and no federal head to fall.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary's position is six literal days, and the sixth is where the cost of surrendering them becomes plain. Genesis 1:31 names an evening and a morning, and the man made that day is the man Paul reasons from in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15. Where the sixth day dissolves into an era or a literary frame, Adam dissolves with it into a symbol of humanity in general — and a symbolic head cannot transmit real guilt, which means the last Adam has no real guilt to answer. The doctrine of sin and the doctrine of salvation are load-bearing on that day.

The second observation is pastoral rather than polemical. The sixth day ended with a benediction — very good — spoken over a world with a man in it. Whatever else the fall has done, it has not revoked the Creator's verdict on His own workmanship, and the sixth hour on Golgotha is God's answer to what the fall did to it. Darkness at noon over the sixth-day creature is the price of restoring the sixth-day benediction.
roots_summary: Hebrew shishshi (H8345), sixth; Greek hektos (G1623), sixth — the day man was made, the hour of noon, the hour darkness fell.
roots_lines: Hebrew shishshi (H8345) — sixth; the sixth day of Gen 1:31 and the sixth year of the land's sabbath cycle.
Greek hektos (G1623) — sixth; the sixth hour of Joh 4:6 and Mat 27:45, and the sixth seal of Rev 6:12.
Jewish reckoning counted hours from sunrise, so the sixth hour is midday — which is what makes the darkness a sign.
usage: “And the evening and the morning were the sixth day” — the day man was made and creation called very good.
“It was about the sixth hour” — the Maker of the world weary at a well.
“From the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land” — noon turned to night over the crucified.

pos: adj. & n. (next after the seventh; rendering Hebrew shemini, Greek ogdoos)
etymology: Saxon eahtotha, from eight. Standing one past the sabbath seven, the eighth is Scripture's day of new beginning — of covenant sign, of naming, and of resurrection appearing.
biblical_def: The eighth day is the day after the completed week, and Scripture loads it with new beginnings. Circumcision, the covenant sign cut into the flesh of Abraham's house, was appointed for it: “And in the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised” (Lev 12:3). So our Lord Himself: “when eight days were accomplished for the circumcising of the child, his name was called JESUS” (Luk 2:21) — the covenant sign and the saving name given on the same day. Paul lists it first among his fleshly credentials, “Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel” (Php 3:5), and then counts the whole column loss for Christ. Peter uses the number differently, of the household carried through the flood: God “saved Noah the eighth person, a preacher of righteousness” (2Pe 2:5) — eight souls, and a world begun again on the far side of the water. The eighth is therefore the ordinal of the fresh start that God Himself makes: after the seven days of the old creation, a day that belongs to the new. It is no accident that the risen Christ appeared to the gathered disciples again after eight days (Joh 20:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines eighth as the ordinal of eight, the next in order after the seventh, and as one part of a thing divided into eight.
webster_full: EIGHTH, a. Noting the number eight; the ordinal of eight.
2. Being one part of eight into which a thing is divided.
EIGHTH, n. An eighth part.
scriptures: Lev 12:3
And in the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.
Luk 2:21
And when eight days were accomplished for the circumcising of the child, his name was called JESUS, which was so named of the angel before he was conceived in the womb.
Php 3:5
Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews; as touching the law, a Pharisee;
And spared not the old world, but saved Noah the eighth person, a preacher of righteousness, bringing in the flood upon the world of the ungodly;
corruption_summary: Circumcision on the eighth day is treated as tribal custom or medical folklore; Scripture presents it as a dated covenant sign, and the New Testament reads its transfer to the heart as the point of the whole institution.
corruption_paragraphs: Two reductions circulate. The first makes the eighth day a hygiene rule discovered early — an ancient people stumbling onto good practice. The second makes it a marker of ethnic identity and nothing more. Both miss what Genesis 17 says it is: a sign of a covenant, cut in blood, on a child who has done neither good nor evil, signifying that the promise runs from God's side before it ever runs from ours. Paul is emphatic that Abraham received the sign after he was justified by faith, which settles the order for good.

The dictionary holds believer's baptism, and precisely for that reason the eighth day must be handled carefully rather than dismissed. What the New Testament does with it is not to relocate the knife but to name what it always pointed at: circumcision made without hands, in the putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh (Col 2:11). The eighth day taught Israel that flesh must be cut before it can be blessed. The gospel says the cutting has fallen on Christ, and the heart is what God now claims.
roots_summary: Hebrew shemini (H8066), eighth; Greek ogdoos (G3590), eighth — the day of circumcision, of naming, and of the eight souls saved through water.
roots_lines: Hebrew shemini (H8066) — eighth; the eighth day of circumcision (Lev 12:3) and the eighth day of the feast, a solemn assembly.
Greek ogdoos (G3590) — eighth; “Noah the eighth person” (2Pe 2:5) and Paul's eighth-day circumcision (Php 3:5).
One day past the sabbath seven, the eighth is the first day of a new week — the day the Lord rose.
usage: “In the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised” — the covenant sign given a date.
“When eight days were accomplished… his name was called JESUS” — sign and saving name together.
“Saved Noah the eighth person” — a world begun again with eight souls.

pos: adj. & n. (next after the eighth; rendering Hebrew teshi'i, Greek enatos)
etymology: Saxon nigotha, from nine. In the Gospels the ninth hour is mid-afternoon — the hour of the evening sacrifice, of the loud cry, and of the temple prayer.
biblical_def: The ninth hour, about three in the afternoon, was the hour of the evening sacrifice in Israel, and the New Testament fastens three scenes to it. First, the death: “And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Mat 27:46) — the true Lamb dying at the very hour the lamb was being bound on the altar in the courts a few hundred yards away. Second, the prayer of the church: “Now Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour” (Act 3:1) — and a man lame from birth walked. Third, the opening of the door to the Gentiles: “at the ninth hour I prayed in my house, and, behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing” (Act 10:30), Cornelius at the hour of sacrifice, receiving the vision that brought Peter to his door. The ninth foundation of the city is a topaz (Rev 21:20). The ordinal thus gathers the whole gospel movement: the sacrifice offered, the church at prayer, and the nations brought in — all at the same appointed hour.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ninth as the ordinal of nine, the next after the eighth, and as one part of a thing divided into nine.
webster_full: NINTH, a. The ordinal of nine; the next preceding the tenth.
2. Constituting or being one of nine equal parts.
NINTH, n. In music, an interval containing an octave and a tone.
scriptures: And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
Act 3:1
Now Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour.
And Cornelius said, Four days ago I was fasting until this hour; and at the ninth hour I prayed in my house, and, behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing,
The fifth, sardonyx; the sixth, sardius; the seventh, chrysolite; the eighth, beryl; the ninth, a topaz; the tenth, a chrysoprasus; the eleventh, a jacinth; the twelfth, an amethyst.
corruption_summary: The cry of the ninth hour is read as despair or as a mistaken Messiah; it is the opening line of Psalm 22, quoted from the cross, and it is the sound of penal substitution being paid.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern treatments of the ninth-hour cry usually take one of two exits. The first makes it a collapse of faith, a good man discovering at the end that no one was there. The second makes it merely a recitation, a dying man reaching for a familiar psalm with no real forsaking behind it. Scripture allows neither. It is genuinely the first line of Psalm 22 — a psalm that ends in worldwide worship, so it is not despair — and it is genuinely a forsaking, because He was made sin for us, and the Father turned from the sin He bore.

Held together, the hour preaches the doctrine. At the hour the evening lamb was slain, the Lamb of God was forsaken so that His people never would be. This is why Hebrews can promise, “I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee” — the forsaking has already happened, once, to Another. Every believer who fears abandonment is being invited to look at three o'clock on that Friday and see the account settled.
roots_summary: Hebrew teshi'i (H8671), ninth; Greek enatos (G1766), ninth — the hour of the evening sacrifice, the loud cry, and the temple prayer.
roots_lines: Hebrew teshi'i (H8671) — ninth; the ninth year and the ninth day of prophetic dating.
Greek enatos (G1766) — ninth; the ninth hour of Mat 27:46, Act 3:1, and Act 10:30.
Hours were counted from sunrise, so the ninth is about three in the afternoon — the hour of the evening oblation (compare Dan 9:21).
usage: “About the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice” — the Lamb forsaken at the hour of sacrifice.
“The hour of prayer, being the ninth hour” — the apostolic church kept the hour and a lame man walked.
“At the ninth hour I prayed in my house” — Cornelius, and the door opened to the nations.

pos: n. (the length of life; the season of maturity; rendering Hebrew yom, seybah, Greek hēlikia)
etymology: From Latin aetas, through French âge. In the Authorized Version age is nearly always a man's span of years, not an epoch of history.
biblical_def: In the Authorized Version age is chiefly personal: the measure of a man's life, and a thing God gives. The LORD promises Abram, “thou shalt go to thy fathers in peace; thou shalt be buried in a good old age” (Gen 15:15), and of David it is written that “he died in a good old age, full of days, riches, and honour” (1Ch 29:28). A good old age is not a biological accident in Scripture; it is a covenant blessing, one of the things promised to those who honour father and mother. Age also marks the point at which a man answers for himself — the parents of the healed blind man push the questioning back onto their son, “he is of age; ask him: he shall speak for himself” (Joh 9:21) — and it marks the point past which nature can no longer help: Sarah “received strength to conceive seed, and was delivered of a child when she was past age, because she judged him faithful who had promised” (Heb 11:11). That last is the doctrine in a sentence. Age is the boundary of what flesh can do, and therefore the place where faith in a promising God does its clearest work.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines age as the whole duration of a being, the latter part of life, a mature or advanced period, and a generation or century of men.
webster_full: AGE, n. The whole duration of a being, whether animal, vegetable or other kind.
2. That part of the duration of a being, which is between its beginning and any given time.
3. The latter part of life, or long continued duration; oldness.
4. A certain period of human life, marked by a difference of state; as the age of infancy, of youth, of manhood.
5. The period when a person is enabled by law to do certain acts for himself; as, to come of age.
scriptures: And thou shalt go to thy fathers in peace; thou shalt be buried in a good old age.
And he died in a good old age, full of days, riches, and honour: and Solomon his son reigned in his stead.
Joh 9:21
But by what means he now seeth, we know not; or who hath opened his eyes, we know not: he is of age; ask him: he shall speak for himself.
Through faith also Sara herself received strength to conceive seed, and was delivered of a child when she was past age, because she judged him faithful who had promised.
corruption_summary: Old age has been reclassified from a crown to a problem — a decline to be delayed, disguised, or shortened — and the honour Scripture commands toward the aged has gone with it.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture calls the hoary head a crown of glory when it is found in the way of righteousness, and commands a man to rise up before the hoary head. A culture that prices usefulness and appearance above all can only read age as loss, and so treats the aged as a cost. From that follows the warehousing of the old, the abandonment of the fifth commandment's duties toward parents, and finally the argument that a life which has stopped producing may be ended early for mercy's sake. Each step is a further denial that the days of a man belong to God and not to his usefulness.

The opposite error is a sentimental cult of youth in the church itself, where the counsel of grey-headed members is quietly set aside for the sake of energy and style. Titus 2 assumes the reverse traffic: aged men sober and sound in faith, aged women teaching the young women. Recover the biblical estimate and both errors fall. A good old age is a blessing to be sought, an honour to be given, and a resource the congregation cannot do without.
roots_summary: Hebrew seybah (H7872), grey hair, old age; Greek hēlikia (G2244), stature or age — the measure of a life, and the boundary where faith takes over from nature.
roots_lines: Hebrew seybah (H7872) — hoary head, grey-headedness, old age; “a good old age” (Gen 15:15) and the crown of glory of Pro 16:31.
Hebrew yom (H3117) — day; in the plural, a man's days, hence his age — “full of days” (1Ch 29:28).
Greek hēlikia (G2244) — age, stature, maturity; “he is of age” (Joh 9:21) and Sarah “past age” (Heb 11:11).
usage: “Thou shalt be buried in a good old age” — length of days named as covenant blessing.
“He is of age; ask him” — the point at which a man answers for himself.
“When she was past age, because she judged him faithful” — where nature ends, faith begins.

pos: adv. (without warning, in a moment; rendering Hebrew pith'om, Greek exaiphnēs, aphnō)
etymology: From Latin subitaneus, from subire, to come up stealthily. Scripture uses it for the two great unannounced arrivals — the Spirit's and the Judge's.
biblical_def: Suddenly in Scripture is the adverb of divine arrival, and it cuts two ways. Malachi promises it of the Messiah: “the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in” (Mal 3:1) — long-awaited and yet, when He came, unannounced and unrecognised by the very courts that kept His feasts. Luke records it of the Spirit: “And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting” (Act 2:2). For the disobedient the same adverb is terror: “Therefore shall his calamity come suddenly; suddenly shall he be broken without remedy” (Pro 6:15). And our Lord makes it the ground of the standing command to watch: “Lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping” (Mar 13:36). The suddenness is not God's carelessness about warning; He has warned for centuries. It is the mercy of a fixed hour withheld, so that His servants are kept awake and His enemies are never able to time their repentance for the last safe moment.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines suddenly as in an unexpected manner, without warning or previous notice, and hastily, without premeditation.
webster_full: SUDDENLY, adv. In an unexpected manner; unexpectedly; hastily; without preparation.
2. Without premeditation.
SUDDEN, a. Happening without previous notice; coming unexpectedly, or without the common preparatives.
scriptures: Mal 3:1

Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in: behold, he shall come, saith the LORD of hosts.
Act 2:2
And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting.
Pro 6:15
Therefore shall his calamity come suddenly; suddenly shall he be broken without remedy.
Lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping.
corruption_summary: Suddenness has been shifted from the Judge to the calendar — date-setting on one side, and on the other the assumption that the world will simply go on, so that the one command attached to the word (watch) is the one thing not done.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors both silence the adverb. The date-setters, from the Millerites to every chart-drawing successor, treat the hour as calculable, which is a flat contradiction of the Lord who said no man knoweth the day nor the hour; each failed date leaves the church more cynical about the coming itself. The practical scoffers of 2 Peter 3 take the other road: all things continue as they were from the beginning, and therefore nothing will suddenly change. The first makes the coming a puzzle; the second makes it a rumour.

The biblical response is neither computation nor complacency but watchfulness — a settled readiness that makes the hour irrelevant. “Lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping” is the Lord's own application, and it is addressed to servants with work in their hands, not to speculators with charts. Malachi's warning stands over the religious in particular: the temple was busy the day He arrived, and busyness was no protection at all.
roots_summary: Hebrew pith'om (H6597), suddenly, in an instant; Greek exaiphnēs (G1810) and aphnō (G869), suddenly — the Spirit's descent and the Judge's arrival.
roots_lines: Hebrew pith'om (H6597) — suddenly, unexpectedly; the calamity of Pro 6:15 and the LORD's coming to His temple (Mal 3:1).
Greek aphnō (G869) — suddenly; the sound from heaven at Pentecost (Act 2:2).
Greek exaiphnēs (G1810) — on a sudden; “lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping” (Mar 13:36).
usage: “The Lord… shall suddenly come to his temple” — long promised, and still unlooked for.
“Suddenly there came a sound from heaven” — the Spirit given without a countdown.
“Lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping” — the command that the adverb exists to enforce.
